cells.tense: You are sitting inside the exchange right now, and the fair call is arriving while you tend it.
cells.ask: Say one true thing about what's fair before the next thing asks for you.
cells.core:
The fairness in a room hasn't needed working out. Something goes one way, someone gives more, and the sense of what's right shows up while it's still happening — clean, no arithmetic, no going back through it later. That reading sits in your body the way balance sits in a person standing up.

So you're tending something and reading the exchange at the same time, and both are still moving. The risk here isn't confusion, it's that you carry the call quietly and nobody hears it — the fairness is real, and it's still private. The next fair word can be spoken where it lands, not saved for a better moment. Say one true thing about what's owed before the next thing asks for you, and stay around for the answer when it comes.
cells.sheetLine: You read what's fair while it's happening. Say it out loud.
cells.verb: reading the fairness in what's passing between people and standing behind the call
cells.place: in the patch of ground where something is still coming up

cells.tense: You are already running the argument that hasn't started, winning it, and paying for it in advance.
cells.ask: Let one exchange this week stay unruled and notice what actually gets taken.
cells.core:
You are ahead of the exchange, not in it. The unfair thing hasn't happened yet, but you've already written the correction, already felt the moment you'd have to step in and set a boundary straight. That foresight is being spent on a scene that may not arrive.

Out ahead like that, the care you're giving turns into supervision. Whoever is inside the thing you're growing gets watched rather than tended — they can feel the ruling before any word comes out of you. The steady version is close by: fairness that stays open long enough for the give and take to move on its own. For one exchange this week, leave the scale alone and see what really happens when you're not holding it.

cells.tense: You are standing one step back from an exchange, keeping it upright by not saying what you see.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you actually noticed, in plain words, and keep it where you can read it.
cells.core:
The reading is still there. You see who gave more, who skimmed, what's owed — you just aren't putting it into the room. So you tend the thing that's growing while a second ledger runs quietly beside it, and the people around you get your even hand instead of your truth.

Fairness doesn't need to be loud, but it does need to be somewhere. Held back long enough, it stops being a judgment you're saving and starts to feel like a distance. That's not a failing, it's what happens to a sense that doesn't get said. The plainest way back is on paper, away from the room: one thing you actually noticed about the exchange, in the words you'd use to yourself. That writing is a place to stand while you figure out where it needs to go.

cells.tense: You are holding the fairness of this exchange steady right now, and you're calling it just keeping the peace.
cells.ask: Tell someone who was there that one recent call about what's fair was yours.
cells.core:
Look at what you did this week: you sat on a remark, you let something slide that cost you, you gave the extra hour without mentioning it. Each one was a decision about what's fair, and you moved them the way a bartender moves glasses — no thought, no credit. From the outside the room stayed even; from the inside you did that. What hasn't happened is you saying so.

That matters more than it sounds. A fair call you don't claim gets absorbed into the background, and then other people's versions of what's fair look just as solid as yours. Pick one recent call and tell someone who was there that it was yours. The claim can be small; it just has to leave your mouth.

attempts.check: The record gives me the card, the seat, and the four statuses with their medicine cards; it does not give me a history, motive, or feeling for the person. The reader may object that Too Much and Too Little feel like opposite failures of the same capacity, or that the ask asks them to do something they can't feel they have — but the ask is only a test gesture, not a measure of them, and it stays useful even if my read lands wrong because it gives them something to try and notice, not a verdict. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'fairness as a feeling that arrives on its own,' which would close the door on anyone who is still catching up to what they owe.

attempts.check: The record hands me the card, the seat, the four statuses and their medicines; it does not hand me one fact about this person's life, so every cell has to work as an offer that a stranger could pick up or set down. A reader may say the four cells should not all sound like the same voice describing the same person, and may reasonably object that no one is 'bracing' or 'quiet' until they recognise it themselves — so the cells describe the shape of the seat under each status, not a verdict about them. The asks stay useful if my read is wrong because each one is a small, finishable gesture that teaches the person something about how they decide what's fair, whether or not the rest lands. The sentence that would serve me more than them is 'you already know what's fair' — it sounds wise and gives the person nothing to hold.
